title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
prompt: Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest palindromic subsequence in `s`. A subsequence is a sequence derived by deleting zero or more characters without changing the order of the remaining characters.

examples.explanation: A single character is trivially its own palindromic subsequence of length 1, the minimum possible input size.

constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters
hints: A neat trick: the longest palindromic subsequence of s is exactly the longest common subsequence of s and its reverse.

Alternatively, think directly in terms of substring bounds: define dp[i][j] as the longest palindromic subsequence within s[i..j]. If s[i] == s[j], those two characters can bookend whatever palindrome is inside s[i+1..j-1].

If s[i] != s[j], the best you can do is the better of dropping one end or the other: max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Fill the table by increasing substring length, since dp[i][j] depends on shorter subranges.

solution.approach: Define dp[i][j] as the length of the longest palindromic subsequence within s[i..j] (inclusive). Every single character is a palindrome of length 1, so dp[i][i] = 1. Fill the table by increasing substring length: if s[i] == s[j], those matching ends can wrap around the best palindrome strictly inside them, so dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2 (treating dp[i+1][j-1] as 0 when i+1 > j-1). If they don't match, the best is whichever of dropping the left or right character does better: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]). The final answer is dp[0][n-1]. This is equivalent to running Longest Common Subsequence between s and its reverse, but computing it directly avoids building the reversed string.
